quote: Es ist {+wahrscheinlich+} [-nicht-] möglich das System aller stetigen und differentiirbaren Funktionen umkehrbar stetig und eindeutig auf das System aller stetigen Funktionen abzubilden.
english: It is probably possible to map the system of all continuous and differentiable functions bijectively and bicontinuously onto the system of all continuous functions.
topic: Miscellaneous notes: uniform distribution of journeys and railway organisation, a probable homeomorphism between differentiable and continuous functions, a paradox derived from tan x = i, an algebraic characterisation of the derivative, and a plan to re-solve Abel's functional equations without assuming differentiability.

triage.modern_statement: Is the space of continuously differentiable (or everywhere differentiable) real functions on an interval, such as [0,1], homeomorphic to the space C[0,1] of all continuous functions? The answer depends on the topology placed on the differentiable functions, which Hilbert did not specify. (a) If C^1[0,1] carries its natural C^1 norm (sup|f| + sup|f'|), both spaces are separable, infinite-dimensional Banach spaces, and the question becomes whether a homeomorphism exists between them. (b) If the differentiable functions carry the sup-norm topology they inherit as a subset of C[0,1], the question is whether that subspace is homeomorphic to C[0,1].
triage.answered_by: Reading (a), C^1 norm: yes. This follows from the Anderson–Kadec theorem (M. I. Kadec, Doklady, 1966-67; R. D. Anderson, 1966): all infinite-dimensional separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic to one another and to Hilbert space ℓ2, so C^1[0,1] ≅ C[0,1]. Reading (b), sup-norm subspace: no. The set of everywhere-differentiable functions inside C[0,1] is coanalytic and not Borel (S. Mazurkiewicz, 1936; Banach had raised the Borel question). A homeomorphism onto the Polish space C[0,1] would make this set Polish, and a Polish subspace of C[0,1] is G_delta and so Borel. That contradiction rules it out. The C^1 functions with the sup norm are a dense, meager subspace and are not completely metrizable, so they are not homeomorphic to C[0,1] either. This second step is standard reasoning, not a result taken from the sources found.

evidence.claim: Anderson–Kadec theorem: all infinite-dimensional separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic.

Anderson proved in 1966 that Hilbert space is homeomorphic to a countable product of lines. Kadec's paper 'On topological equivalence of separable Banach spaces' (Doklady) led to the result that all separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic.

Statement of the Anderson-Kadec theorem: every infinite-dimensional, separable, locally convex, complete linear space is homeomorphic to ℓ2. Lists the papers that led to it (Kadec, Anderson, Bessaga–Pełczyński).
Banach pointed out that the set D of functions in C[0,1] differentiable at every point is coanalytic, and asked whether D is a Borel set.
Mazurkiewicz showed that the subset of C[0,1] consisting of the differentiable functions is an example of a non-Borel set in descriptive set theory.

triage.why: This is a real research question in infinite-dimensional topology, not one of Hilbert's published problems. Under the most natural modern reading (C^1 with its own Banach norm), Hilbert's corrected guess ('probably possible') turned out to be true: it is a special case of the Anderson–Kadec theorem of 1966-67. If differentiable functions instead keep the sup-norm topology, the answer is negative: Mazurkiewicz's 1936 non-Borel result rules out a homeomorphism for everywhere-differentiable functions, and a completeness argument (my inference) does the same for C^1. Confidence is medium for three reasons. Hilbert's note does not say which topology he meant. 'stetig und differentiirbar' could mean C^1 or merely everywhere differentiable. And no source found discusses Hilbert's note itself. The underlying problem is fully settled, so it is not an active research area, although the descriptive set theory of classes of differentiable functions is still studied.
